It is situated on [[Long Island Sound]] at the mouth of the [[Housatonic River]]. The town is part of the [[Greater Bridgeport Planning Region, Connecticut|Greater Bridgeport Planning Region]] and the [[Greater Bridgeport|Bridgeport–Stamford–Norwalk Metropolitan Statistical Area]] a component of the greater [[New York metropolitan area]]. It was settled by the [[Puritans]] in 1639. The population was 52,355 as of the [[2020 United States census|2020 census]].{{cite web |url=https://data.census.gov/cedsci/profile?g=0600000US0900174190|title=Census - Geography Profile: Stratford town, Fairfield County, Connecticut |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]] |access-date=December 21, 2021}} It is bordered on the west by [[Bridgeport, Connecticut|Bridgeport]], to the north by [[Trumbull, Connecticut|Trumbull]] and [[Shelton, Connecticut|Shelton]], and on the east by [[Milford, Connecticut|Milford]] (across the Housatonic River). Stratford has a historical legacy in aviation, the military, and theater. ==History== [[File:PostcardStratfordCTLibrary1909.jpg|thumb|right|250px|Stratford Public Library, as seen in a 1909 postcard]] [[File:Trolley exploring - an electric railroad guide to historic and picturesque places about New York, New Jersey, and New England (1904) (14760880155).jpg|thumb|Street of the Triple Elms, as seen in the 1890s]] ===Founding and Puritan era=== Stratford was founded in 1639 by Puritan leader Reverend [[Adam Blakeman]], [[William Beardsley (settler)|William Beardsley]], and either 16 families (according to legend) or approximately 35 families (suggested by later research) who had recently arrived in [[Connecticut Colony]] from [[England]] seeking religious freedom. In 1639 the General Court in Hartford made reference to the town as the "new plantation at '''Pequannock'''".{{cite web|url=http://www.stratfordhistoricalsociety.org/stratfordhistory.html|title=Stratford History|publisher=Stratford Historical Society|access-date=April 4, 2018}} In 1640 the community was known as '''Cupheag''', a Native American [[Paugusset|Paugussett]] word meaning "at the enclosed place" or "place of shelter".{{cite web|url=https://library.si.edu/digital-library/book/indianplacenames00hude|title=Indian Place Names of New England|author=John C. Huden|date=1962|work=library.si.edu|access-date=April 4, 2018}} By April 13, 1643, the growing town was known as '''Stratford''', in honor of [[Stratford-upon-Avon]] in England.{{cite book|title=The Connecticut Magazine: An Illustrated Monthly|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qoEyAQAAMAAJ&pg=PA334 |year=1903|publisher=Connecticut Magazine Company|page=334}} Stratford is one of many towns in the northeastern [[Thirteen Colonies|American colonies]] founded as part of the [[Puritan migration to New England (1620–1640)|Great Migration]] in the 1630s when Puritan families fled an increasingly polarized England in the decade before the [[English Civil War|civil war]] between [[Charles I of England|Charles I]] and [[Parliament of the United Kingdom|Parliament]]. Some of the Stratford settlers were from families who had first moved from England to the [[Netherlands]] to seek religious freedom, like their predecessors on the ''[[Mayflower]]'', and decided to come to the [[New World]] when their children began to adopt [[Dutch people|Dutch]] culture and language. Like other Puritan or [[Pilgrims (Plymouth Colony)|Pilgrim]] towns founded during this time, early Stratford was a place where church leadership and town leadership were united under the pastor of the church, in this case Reverend Blakeman. The goal of the communities was to create perfect outposts of religious idealism where the wilderness would separate them from the interference of kings, parliaments, or any other secular authority. During the [[witch trials in Connecticut]], [[Goody Bassett]] was hanged in Stratford in May 1651.{{Cite news |date=2023-11-03 |title=Goody Bassett Exonerated! |url=https://stratfordcrier.com/goody-bassett-exonerated-plaque/ |access-date=2025-10-17 |work=Stratford Crier |language=en}} Blakeman ruled Stratford until his death in 1665, but as the second generation of Stratford grew up, many of the children rejected what they perceived as the exceptional austerity of the town's founders. They and later generations sought to change the religious dictums of their elders, and the [[utopia]]n nature of Stratford and similar communities was gradually replaced with more standard colonial administration. By the late 17th century, the Connecticut government had assumed political control over Stratford. Many descendants of the original founding Puritan families remain in Stratford today after over 350 years; for centuries they often intermarried within the original small group of 17th century Pilgrim families. Despite its Puritan origins, Stratford was the site of the first [[Anglicanism|Anglican]] church in Connecticut, founded in 1707 and ministered by the [[Samuel Johnson|Rev. Dr. Samuel Johnson]].[http://www.christchurchstratford.org/history.htm] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929080827/http://www.christchurchstratford.org/history.htm|date=September 29, 2007}} Settlers from Stratford founded other cities and towns including [[Newark, New Jersey]] established in 1666 by members of the Stratford founding families who believed the town's religious purity had been compromised by the changes after Blakeman's death. [[Cambria, New York]] (now [[Lockport, New York]]) and other towns were founded or expanded around new churches by Stratford descendants taking part in the westward migration. [[Gerald Ford|President Gerald Ford]] was a descendant of one of the Stratford founding families which was led by . ===Towns created from Stratford=== Stratford was one of the two principal settlements in [[southwestern Connecticut]], the other being [[Fairfield, Connecticut|Fairfield]]. Over time it gave rise to several new towns which broke off and incorporated separately. These towns were created from parts of Stratford: * [[Shelton, Connecticut|Shelton]] (originally Ripton) in 1789; in 1789 Ripton Parish separated from Stratford and became the Town of Huntington :*[[Monroe, Connecticut|Monroe]] created from Huntington in 1823 * [[Nichols, Connecticut|Nichols]] (originally Unity in 1725, then North Stratford in 1744) * [[Long Hill, Trumbull, Connecticut|Long Hill]], (merged with Unity to form North Stratford in 1744) :*[[Trumbull, Connecticut|Trumbull]], North Stratford separated from Stratford and became the town of Trumbull in 1797 * [[Bridgeport, Connecticut|Bridgeport]] (also partly from Fairfield) in 1821 ===Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries=== A trolley was built connecting [[Lordship, Connecticut|Lordship]] to Bridgeport in 1914, connecting the resort area to the neighboring city.{{cite web | url=https://www.lordshiphistory.com/TROLLEYwebpage.html | title=Lordship Trolley }} ==Geography== According to the [[United States Census Bureau]], the town has a total area of {{convert|19.9|sqmi}}, of which {{convert|17.6|sqmi}} is land and {{convert|2.3|sqmi}}, or 11.52%, is water. Stratford has a minimum elevation of zero feet above sea level along its coastline, with a maximum altitude of {{convert|295|ft}} near its northern border,U.S. Geological Survey 7.5 minute topographic map series, Ansonia quadrangle and an average elevation of {{convert|23|ft|m}}.{{Citation needed|date=August 2010}} ===Coastline and islands=== The town contains five islands, all in the Housatonic River. These are [[Carting Island]], [[Long Island (Connecticut)|Long Island]], [[Peacock Island (Connecticut)|Peacock Island]], and [[Pope's Flat]] north of [[Interstate 95 in Connecticut|Interstate 95]], as well as [[Goose Island (Connecticut)|Goose Island]]. None of the islands are habitable because of their low elevations. A sixth island known as Brinsmade Island washed away prior to 1964.{{cite book |author=Lewis G. Knapp |title=Stratford and the Sea |place=Charleston, SC |publisher=Arcadia |year=2002 }} ===Beaches=== '''Long Beach''' – Approximately {{convert|1.5|mi|km}} long, the eastern end of the beach is open to the public and has parking and lifeguards. The central part of the beach is a nature preserve whose land is set aside for wildlife, particularly nesting raptors like [[American kestrel]]s and [[osprey]]s. The western end of the beach was once the site of about 40 cottages, which were abandoned because of the town's discontinuation of the lease to the land. The cottages were demolished in fall 2010. [[File:Stratfpt.jpg|thumb|[[Stratford Point Light]]]] '''Russian Beach''' – Located between Long and Short beaches, Russian Beach has parking and the Point-No-Point walkway. Fishing is allowed, as is swimming although the beach has no lifeguards. '''Short Beach''' – Short Beach Park is {{convert|30|acre|m2}} in size and sits at the mouth of the Housatonic River. It has three picnic pavilions, basketball courts, tennis courts, volleyball courts, a handicapped-accessible playground, a skateboard park, a lighted softball field, a soccer field, two baseball fields and a lacrosse field. The beach has {{convert|1000|ft|m}} of frontage with a concession stand, bathrooms, a deck and lifeguards. The park is home to Short Beach Golf Course, a nine-hole par-3 course. ===Great Salt Marsh=== The Great Meadows Unit of the [[Stewart B. McKinney National Wildlife Refuge]] is a key bird migration stopover. The open water area of the Great Salt Marsh is known as Lewis Gut. [[File:ParadiseGreen2020.jpg|thumb|upright=2|right|Paradise Green Park; shops in Paradise Green include a pharmacy, ice cream shop, restaurants, and a bakery]] ===Neighborhoods=== * Beaver Dam * Birdseye * Floral Park * Hawley Lane (shared with [[Trumbull, Connecticut|Trumbull]]) * [[Stratford Center Historic District|Historic District]] * Hollister Heights * [[Lordship, Connecticut|Lordship]] * Long Beach * [[Oronoque, Connecticut|Oronoque]] * Oronoque Hills * Oronoque Village * Paradise Green * Peck's Mill * [[Putney, Connecticut|Putney]] * South End * Stony Brook Gardens * [[Stratford Center Historic District|Stratford Center]] * [[Stratford Downtown, Connecticut|Stratford Downtown]] * Success Village * Wooster Park ===Roosevelt Forest=== Located in the north end of Stratford, this {{convert|250|acre|km2|adj=on}} site is primarily a mixed [[deciduous forest]], with some wetlands and ponds. Named for [[Franklin D. Roosevelt|President Franklin D. Roosevelt]], it was set aside in the 1930s, when much of the infrastructure was created as a [[Works Progress Administration]] project. The forest includes campsites with cooking pits, picnic tables, and walking trails. ===Superfund sites=== [[File:Raymarkstratfordcleanup1.jpg|thumb|Cleanup of a Raymark Industries Superfund site, in Stratford]] Stratford is the location of two [[Superfund]] sites designated by the [[United States Environmental Protection Agency]] including a variety of locations related to asbestos dumping and disposal by [[Raybestos|Raymark Industries]], whose manufacturing was previously headquartered in Stratford, and the former [[Stratford Army Engine Plant]]. The Raymark site is on the EPA's [[National Priorities List]]. Stratford Army Engine Plant is not on the National Priorities list, but is being cleaned up by the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]]. From 1919 to 1989, Raymark manufactured [[brake pad]]s and other [[friction]] products for the automobile industry under the name [[Raybestos]]. The company disposed of wastes containing [[lead]], [[asbestos]], [[Polychlorinated biphenyl|PCBs]], and other hazardous substances at its Stratford manufacturing plant. Raymark dried the waste material and made it available for use as fill material for lawns, playgrounds, and schoolyards. In 1993, the EPA and the Connecticut Department of Environmental Protection began working together to complete the cleanup of contamination Raymark left in Stratford. EPA completed its cleanup of the contaminated residential properties in 1995 and the former Raymark plant property in 1997. Plans for cleanup of the Ferry Creek area and surrounding properties where additional Raymark waste was historically disposed are being developed by the EPA.[http://www.epa.gov/ne/pr/1997/pr0110b.html epa.gov: U.S. Sues Raymark Industries for Estimated $192 Million Cleanup of Connecticut Superfund Site] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030128210208/http://www.epa.gov/ne/pr/1997/pr0110b.html |date=January 28, 2003 }} The cost of cleaning up the Raymark Site is estimated to have exceeded $200 million.[http://www.epa.gov/ne/pr/1998/082798.html epa.gov: Settlement Protects Settling Stratford Homeowners from Superfund Costs] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061009183050/http://www.epa.gov/ne/pr/1998/082798.html |date=October 9, 2006 }} ==Demographics== {{US Census population |1820= 3438 |1850= 2040 |1860= 2294 |1870= 3032 |1880= 4251 |1890= 2608 |1900= 3657 |1910= 5712 |1920= 12347 |1930= 19212 |1940= 22580 |1950= 33428 |1960= 45012 |1970= 49775 |1980= 50541 |1990= 49389 |2000= 49976 |2010= 51384 |2020= 52355 |footnote=U.S. Decennial Census{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/decennial-census.html |title=Census of Population and Housing |publisher=Census.gov |access-date=November 3, 2021 }} }} {{See also|List of Connecticut locations by per capita income}} As of the [[2010 United States census|census]]{{cite web |url=https://www.census.gov |publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]] |access-date=January 31, 2008 |title=U.S. Census website }} of 2010, there were 51,384 people, 20,095 households, and 13,614 families residing in the town. The population density was {{convert|2919.5|PD/sqmi|PD/km2|sp=us|adj=off}}. There were 21,091 housing units at an average density of {{convert|1,198.4|/sqmi|/km2|sp=us|adj=off}}. The racial makeup of the town was 76.4% [[White (U.S. Census)|White]], 14.3% [[African American (U.S. Census)|Black]] or [[Race (United States Census)|African American]], 0.2% [[Native American (U.S. Census)|Native American]], 2.4% [[Asian (U.S. Census)|Asian]], 0.1% [[Pacific Islander (U.S. Census)|Pacific Islander]], 4.2% from [[Race (United States Census)|other races]], and 2.5% from two or more races. [[Hispanic (U.S. Census)|Hispanic]] or [[Latino (U.S. Census)|Latino]] of any race were 13.8% of the population. There were 20,095 households, of which 28.2% had children under the age of 18 living with them, 49.1% were [[Marriage|married couples]] living together, 14.2% had a female householder with no husband present, and 32.3% were non-families. 27.3% of all households were made up of individuals, and 13.5% had someone living alone who was 65 years of age or older. The average household size was 2.54 and the average family size was 3.11. In the town, the population was spread out, with 23.0% under the age of 18, 5.8% from 18 to 24, 28.5% from 25 to 44, 23.5% from 45 to 64, and 19.2% who were 65 years of age or older. The median age was 42.2 years. For every 100 females, there were 89.0 males. For every 100 females age 18 and over, there were 85.6 males. The median income for a household in the town was $53,494, and the median income for a family was $64,364. Males had a median income of $45,552 versus $34,575 for females. The [[per capita income]] for the town was $26,501. About 3.5% of families and 5.0% of the population were below the [[poverty line]], including 5.6% of those under age 18 and 5.8% of those age 65 or over. ==Economy== ===Top employers=== Top employers in Stratford according to the town's 2025 Comprehensive Annual Financial Report{{cite web|url=https://files-backend.assets.thrillshare.com/documents/asset/uploaded_file/3632/Stratford/af90f949-251c-4a6a-9dd6-807bfee3c1ac/Final-ACFR-FY25.pdf?disposition=inline|title=Town of Stratford Comprehensive Annual Financial Report For the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 2025|publisher=Town of Stratford|access-date=March 30, 2026}} {| class="wikitable" |- ! # ! Employer ! # of Employees |- |1 |Lockheed Martin-[[Sikorsky Aircraft]] |5,734 |- |2 |Town of Stratford |1,613 |- |3 | [[FedEx Ground]] | 1,200 |- |4 | Lord Chamberlain | 482 |- |5 | Burns Construction | 405 |- |6 | Ashcroft Holdings | 400 |- |7 | EnCon | 317 |- |8 | Connecticut Distributor | 305 |- |9 | Nuovo Pasta | 275 |- |10 | Bridgeport Fittings | 241 |} In 1939, one of the world's first successful commercial [[helicopter]]s was developed in Stratford by [[Igor Sikorsky]] and flown at his plant.[http://www.centennialofflight.gov/essay/Rotary/Sikorsky_VS300/HE8.htm] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081112050442/http://www.centennialofflight.gov/essay/Rotary/Sikorsky_VS300/HE8.htm|date=November 12, 2008}} His company, [[Sikorsky Aircraft|Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation]], is still the town's largest employer. Also in 1939, [[Lycoming Engines]] produced [[Curtiss-Wright|Wright]] [[radial engine]]s here. After [[World War II]], the plant was converted to produce [[turbine]]s. The Vought-Sikorsky Aircraft Division in Stratford built 7,829 [[F4U]] fighters from 1940 to 1952, including the prototype. The planes were in extensive combat in the Pacific Theatre of operations during World War II, and played a supporting role in the [[Korean War]]. A Corsair sits on a pedestal at the airport as a memorial to the war effort.{{cite web |url=http://www.uswarplanes.net/corsair.html |title=Corsair |publisher=Uswarplanes.net |date=May 29, 1940 |access-date=May 19, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081121032514/http://www.uswarplanes.net/corsair.html |archive-date=November 21, 2008 |url-status=dead }} The Stratford Eagles Composite Squadron, [[Civil Air Patrol]], is based in Stratford, at the Sikorsky Memorial Airport. [[Athletic Brewing Company]], the leading U.S. manufacturer of [[Non-alcoholic drink|non-alcoholic]] [[craft beer]], with a 61% market share in 2021 is based in Stratford.{{Cite news|date=January 13, 2021|title=Celebrity Backers Are Making Nonalcoholic Beer a Hot Investment|language=en|work=Bloomberg.com|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-01-13/athletic-brewing-non-alcoholic-beer-a-hot-celebrity-investment-dry-january|access-date=April 11, 2021}} ===Sikorsky Aircraft=== [[File:CSA-2005-05-05-102937.jpg|right|thumb|Sikorsky Aircraft [[Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk|Black Hawk]] helicopters in Iraq in 2005]] Stratford is home to the headquarters of Sikorsky Aircraft, a [[Lockheed Martin]] (LMT) subsidiary founded by [[Igor Sikorsky]], developer of the first successful American helicopter. Every [[Marine One]] (the helicopter of the [[president of the United States]]) has been manufactured in Stratford since 1957. On July 20, 2015, Lockheed Martin announced an agreement to purchase Sikorsky Aircraft from UTC for $9 billion.{{cite web|author1=Christopher Drew|author2=Chad Bray|date=July 20, 2015|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/07/21/business/dealbook/lockheed-martin-to-buy-sikorsky-aircraft-for-9-billion.html|title=Lockheed Martin to Buy Sikorsky Aircraft for $9 Billion|website=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=December 5, 2016}} ===Stratford Army Engine Plant=== The [[Stratford Army Engine Plant]] (SAEP) was a U.S. Army Tank-Automotive and Armaments Command installation and manufacturing facility, located along the Housatonic River and Main Street opposite Sikorsky Airport. Because of the [[Base Realignment and Closure]] actions of the [[United States Department of Defense]], closure of the plant was recommended in July 1995. The SAEP closed on September 30, 1998. For the next 11 years the Army was involved with "Team Stratford" to develop the property. The [[United States Army]], which owns the {{convert|78|acre|m2|adj=on}} site, auctioned it off on March 19, 2008,{{cite web |url=http://www.townofstratford.com/controls//eventview.aspx?MODE=SINGLE&ID=64 |title=Event Viewer |publisher=Townofstratford.com |access-date=January 2, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717082800/http://www.townofstratford.com/controls//eventview.aspx?MODE=SINGLE&ID=64 |archive-date=July 17, 2011 }} with a winning bid of $9,612,000 which also includes the {{convert|1,720,000|ft2|m2|adj=on}} facility of over fifty buildings. The bid failed to be paid off and is being placed for rebid. Robert Hartmann of Hartmann Development has a $1 billion plan to develop the former Army engine plant into a destination resort.{{cite web|url=http://www.ctpost.com/default/article/Former-Army-plant-proposed-as-destination-resort-720226.php |title=Former Army plant proposed as destination resort - Connecticut Post |publisher=Ctpost.com |date=October 23, 2010 |access-date=January 2, 2011}} ==Transportation== [[File:P1010073 M-2 8731 Stratford.jpg|thumb|[[Metro-North Railroad|Metro-North]] [[New Haven Line]] train at [[Stratford station (Connecticut)|Stratford station]]]] ===Air=== Although owned by the City of Bridgeport, [[Sikorsky Memorial Airport]] is located in Stratford. The {{convert|800|acre|km2|adj=on}} facility includes two paved runways (both under 4800 feet), a helipad, and two hangars. It provides helicopter service to New York and the [[Downtown Manhattan Heliport]] and is used as a landing site for blimps and small aircraft. In 2019, 155 aircraft were based at the airport, with an average of 136 operations per day.''[https://www.airnav.com/airport/KBDR AirNav: KBDR]'' ===Rail=== [[Stratford station (Connecticut)|Stratford (Metro-North station)]] is a stop on the [[New Haven Line]], {{convert|59|mi|km}} east of [[Grand Central Terminal]]. Average travel time into [[Manhattan|Manhattan, New York]] is about 90 minutes. The station platforms are only long enough to handle four cars and the station has limited parking for fewer than 300 vehicles. It has three ticket machines, a bus connection to neighboring Bridgeport, and handicapped access. ===Roads=== Stratford is served by several major highways including [[Interstate 95 in Connecticut|Interstate 95]] ([[Connecticut Turnpike]]), [[U.S. Route 1 in Connecticut|U.S. Route 1]] ([[Boston Post Road]]) (Boston Avenue and Barnum Avenue), the [[Merritt Parkway]] ([[Connecticut Route 15|Route 15]]), [[Connecticut Route 108|Route 108]] (Nichols Avenue and King Street), [[Connecticut Route 110|Route 110]] (East Main Street and River Road), [[Connecticut Route 113|Route 113]] (Lordship Boulevard and Main Street), and [[Connecticut Route 130|Route 130]] (Stratford Avenue and Ferry Boulevard). ====Interstate 95 toll booths==== In January 1983 a truck slammed into a line of cars waiting to pay a toll on [[Interstate 95 in Connecticut|Interstate 95]] in Stratford, killing seven people. The accident was one of the reasons toll booths were removed throughout the state.{{cite web|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9E02E0DE1E38F931A15752C0A965948260 |title=nytimes.com: Dead Identified In Turnpike Crash |location=Connecticut |work=The New York Times |date=January 22, 1983 |access-date=January 2, 2011}} ==Government== {| class="wikitable" style="float:right; margin:1em; font-size:95%;" |+ Stratford town vote

changed to a mayor-council type of government. The first mayor, James Miron, was elected in November 2005 to a four-year term. The second mayor was John Harkins.{{cite web |url=http://www.townofstratford.com/content/1302/1944/21242.aspx |title=Stratford, Connecticut - Mayor Harkins Biography |publisher=Townofstratford.com |access-date=January 2, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101005061133/http://www.townofstratford.com/content/1302/1944/21242.aspx |archive-date=October 5, 2010 }} The town has a ten-member town council, elected by district to two-year terms. It appoints one of its members to serve as chairman. The mayor and the council are responsible for setting policy through the enactment of ordinances and resolutions. The department responds to approximately 8500 calls annually.[22]{{Citation needed|date=October 2018}} ===Fire department=== Established in 1909, the fire department operates out of four stations located throughout the town. The fire department staffs four engine companies, a truck company, a rescue unit, and a shift commander along with several specialized response units. The department responds to approximately 6000 calls annually.[http://www.townofstratford.com/content/1302/402/611/default.aspx] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100721233957/http://www.townofstratford.com/content/1302/402/611/default.aspx|date=July 21, 2010}} ===Police department=== Created in 1917, the Stratford Police Department has a force of 98 officers. The department's units include arson investigation, crime prevention, a identification & forensic unit, and narcotics & vice. Stratford also has a boat patrol, a [[Police dog|K-9 unit]],{{cite web |url=http://www.townofstratford.com/content/1302/402/621/default.aspx |title=Stratford, Connecticut - Police Department |publisher=Townofstratford.com |date=December 22, 2010 |access-date=January 2, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101114013003/http://www.townofstratford.com/content/1302/402/621/default.aspx |archive-date=November 14, 2010 }} and an animal control unit.{{cite web |author=Michael Romsky |url=http://www.stratfordac.org/ |title=Stratford Animal Control | Home |publisher=Stratfordac.org |access-date=January 2, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110101185522/http://www.stratfordac.org/ |archive-date=January 1, 2011 }} ==Education== ===Public education=== Public education in Stratford is managed by the Stratford Board of Education, which operates 13 schools: two high schools, two middle schools, and nine elementary schools.[http://www.stratfordk12.org/ Stratford Public Schools] The district has about 6,800 students and 1,095 staff including 577 teachers, counselors, and specialists.{{cite web|url=https://edsight.ct.gov/Output/District/HighSchool/1380011_201819.pdf |title=Connecticut SDE District Profile: Stratford School District|publisher=edsighy.ct.gov |date=October 1, 2018 |access-date=June 3, 2020}} ====High schools==== * [[Frank Scott Bunnell High School]] * [[Stratford High School (Connecticut)|Stratford High School]] * A.L.P.H.A. Notably, it displays the [[Lycoming T53]] jet engine, designed by Dr. [[Anselm Franz]] and manufactured at the [[Stratford Army Engine Plant]]. [[File:Short Beach II.jpg|thumb|Oysters at low tide; Short Beach is open from sunrise to sunset]] [[File:Short Beach I.jpg|thumb|A tree on Short Beach in Stratford, Connecticut]] ===Boothe Memorial Park=== {{Main|Boothe Memorial Park}} The {{convert|30|acre|m2|adj=on}} Boothe homestead in the Putney area of Stratford is a rolling parkland containing the original Boothe homestead and an eclectic assortment of buildings collected by the Boothe brothers during their lives and added to by the Friends of Boothe. A tollbooth that was in service from 1940 to 1988 on Connecticut's [[Merritt Parkway]] is on display in Boothe Memorial Park. ===Shakespeare Festival Theatre=== {{Main|American Shakespeare Theatre}} In 1955 Stratford became home to the American Shakespeare Theatre, an 1,100-seat theater{{citation needed|date=November 2014}} with grounds on the [[Housatonic River]]. The theater featured noteworthy actors including [[Katharine Hepburn]], [[James Earl Jones]], [[Paul Newman]], [[Jessica Tandy]], [[Jane Alexander]], [[Hal Holbrook]], [[Roddy McDowall]], [[Nina Foch]], and [[Will Geer]]. [[John Houseman]] served as its artistic director during the late 1950s. The company operating the theater ceased operations in the mid-1980s, and the building has been vacant since then. In February 2005, the Town of Stratford received the deed for the Stratford Festival Shakespeare Theater from the state of Connecticut. In 2006 it selected a New York City development company to reopen the theater as a tourist destination, but the company's contract was terminated in July 2007 because of lack of progress. In 2019 the theatre burned to the ground.{{Cite web|url=https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/Fire-Destroys-Historic-Shakespeare-Theatre-in-Stratford-504285771.html|title = Fire Destroys Historic Shakespeare Theatre in Stratford| date=January 13, 2019 }} === Stratford Library Shakespeare === Since 2002, the [[Hudson Shakespeare Company]] has presented an annual showing of their [[Shakespeare in the Park]] in the amphitheater behind the Stratford Library. ===Sites on the National Register of Historic Places=== * [[Boothe Homestead]] (1985) * [[Captain David Judson House|Capt. Booth House]] (1992) * [[Sterling Homestead]] (1976) * [[Stratford Center Historic District]] (1983) * [[Stratford Point Light]] (1990), a lighthouse * [[Washington Bridge (Connecticut)|Washington Bridge]] (2004) ===Sterling House=== Since 1932, Sterling House has served as a community center for Stratford. Housed in a donated 1886 [[Romanesque architecture|Romanesque]] mansion that was previously the home of [[John William Sterling]], it hosts recreational and leisure activities for adults and children, charity events, and volunteer activities. The grounds include a gazebo, a rose garden, and a {{convert|2|acre|m2|adj=on}} field. ==Sports== Stratford is home to the [[Connecticut Brakettes]] women's [[fastpitch softball]] team. Formed in 1947 as the Raybestos Girl All-Stars, and later called the Raybestos Brakettes, they became known as the Stratford Brakettes in 1985 after Raybestos ceased its sponsorship. The team has posted 3,242 victories in 3,607 games played, as well as three world championships and 28 national [[Amateur Softball Association|A.S.A.]] (USA Softball) championships including a record eight consecutive titles from 1971 to 1978.{{cite web|url=http://www.stratfordbrakettes.com/|title=Brakettes Archives|access-date=October 21, 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090302010411/http://www.stratfordbrakettes.com/|archive-date=March 2, 2009}}{{cite web|last=Hays|first=Graham|title=The saga of the Stratford Brakettes|url=https://www.espn.com/espn/page2/story?page=hays/080718|date=July 21, 2008|access-date=October 20, 2009|publisher=[[ESPN]]}} They captured three consecutive titles in 2002, 2003, and 2004. Their most recent title was in 2006.[http://www.brakettes.com/national_tournaments.htm brakettes.com: National Championship results] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070218102523/http://www.brakettes.com/national_tournaments.htm |date=February 18, 2007 }}{{cite web|url=http://brakettes.com/history/|title=Brakettes (history)|access-date=October 21, 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090706064754/http://brakettes.com/history/|archive-date=July 6, 2009}} There are 19 former members in the National Softball Hall of Fame and 11 have been Olympians.{{cite web|url=http://www.stratfordbrakettes.com/alltime_roster.htm|title=Brakettes All-Time Roster|access-date=October 20, 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120225165159/http://www.stratfordbrakettes.com/alltime_roster.htm|archive-date=February 25, 2012}} The Brakettes play at Frank DeLuca Hall of Fame Field. ==Media== ===Movies filmed in Stratford=== Movies filmed at least partially in Stratford:{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/search/title|title=IMDb: Most Popular Titles With Location Matching "Stratford, Connecticut, USA"|work=IMDb|access-date=December 5, 2016}} * ''Butterfield Eight'' (1960){{cite web|url=http://lordshiphistory.com/MOVIESwebpage.html |title=The History of Lordship! |publisher=Lordshiphistory.com |access-date=January 2, 2011}} * ''The Battle'' (2001) * ''Carnauba: A Son's Memoir'' (2001) * ''Zero Day'' (2003) * ''Das Kraftei'' – Raketenjäger ME 163 Komet (2004) * ''Boxes'' (2005), a short film, not to be confused with ''Boxes'' (2007) * ''Store'' (2006) * ''Listen to Your Heart'' (2009) * ''All Good Things'' (2010) * ''Daddy for Lunch'' (2010) * ''Sketchy Future'' (2010) * ''Sicarii'' (2011) * ''Chang Can Dunk'' (2023) ===Newspapers=== Stratford is served by Bridgeport's daily ''[[Connecticut Post]]'' and by the weekly digital Stratford Crier.
